title: Information in Spanish on YouTube about Covid-19 vaccines
screen_reason: Reports the share of items in a fully coded sample judged false: hoaxes and conspiracy theories were identified in 2 of the 118 most-viewed Spanish-language YouTube videos on COVID-19 vaccines (1.7%). The paper also gives the view counts of those 2 videos and of the whole corpus, allowing an exact view-weighted share.

estimates.country: Mexico (35.6%), USA (15.3%), Colombia (12.7%), Spain (11.0%), Argentina (10.2%), Chile (4.2%), Germany (3.4%), United Kingdom (3.4%), Peru (2.5%), Venezuela (0.8%), Dominican Republic (0.8%)
estimates.date: Search performed 9 February 2021; videos uploaded 18 March 2020 to 5 February 2021
estimates.measure_type: % of the most-viewed Spanish-language YouTube videos on COVID-19 vaccines that contained hoaxes or conspiracy theories
estimates.value_raw: 2/118 videos (1.7%): "Hoaxes/conspiracy theories were identified in 1.7% of the videos"; "Hoaxes and conspiracy theories were detected in 2 videos"
estimates.denominator: 118 most-viewed Spanish-language YouTube videos returned by the searches 'Vacuna Covid', 'Vacuna coronavirus' and 'Vacuna Covid19' on 9 February 2021, after excluding unavailable, non-Spanish, duplicate and off-topic videos
estimates.definition: A video counted in the numerator if the two independent raters recorded the presence of 'myths and conspiracy theories' content; the two flagged videos asserted, respectively, that compulsory vaccination hides a dictatorial agenda and that the coronavirus was created in a laboratory by the WHO (with reference to the vaccine as the 'mark of the Beast').
estimates.misinfo_def: The paper does not define misinformation formally; it works from the WHO 'infodemic' framing ('overabundance of information, some accurate and some not') and codes a video-content category of 'myths and conspiracy theories' / 'hoaxes'.
estimates.source_quote: Hoaxes and conspiracy theories were detected in 2 videos; such videos were produced by media and users, on May and August 2020, from the USA and Spain; by type of publication, they were news and material created by the user, their median (range) duration was 524 seconds (243–805), and garnered 616,191 views, 23,477 likes, 2,458 dislikes and 7,790 comments.
estimates.page_loc: Results, p. 3917-3918; headline figure also in the Abstract ('Hoaxes/conspiracy theories were identified in 1.7% of the videos')
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Two authors (both physicians: Preventive Medicine and Primary Care) independently viewed and coded every video. Inter-rater agreement is reported only for MESSAGE TONE: total agreement except on 2 videos, kappa = 0.971, disagreements resolved by consensus. No reliability statistic is reported for the hoax/conspiracy-theory content variable specifically. Classification is against the raters' clinical judgement, not against a fact-check database or source list.
estimates.moderator_quote: The keywords "Vacuna Covid," "Vacuna coronavirus," and "Vacuna Covid19" were searched on YouTube on 9 February 2021 using a cleared browser. The results were sorted by the number of views since this is a common and accepted procedure when investigating YouTube videos. After applying the exclusion criteria (not available for viewing, language other than Spanish, videos that were duplicated, and videos that did not provide information on Covid-19 vaccines), the 118 most widely viewed videos were selected.
estimates.notes: denom_selection=curated because the corpus is a rank-truncated top-N-by-views set (the 118 most viewed after exclusions), not a random or complete sample of Spanish COVID-19-vaccine videos; a most-viewed set is dominated by mainstream media (57.6% of videos, 55.0% of views), which pushes the misinformation share down. breadth coded 'fabricated': the numerator is restricted to hoaxes and conspiracy theories and does NOT include merely misleading or anti-vaccine content - the single video with an outright NEGATIVE tone (0.8%) is a separate variable and is not necessarily false, and the 13.6% ambiguous-tone videos are not counted either. Note the corpus is defined by language (Spanish) and spans 11 countries, so country_norm is Multi-country. With only 2 events out of 118 the estimate is very imprecise (95% CI roughly 0.2-6%).

estimates.country: Mexico, USA, Colombia, Spain, Argentina, Chile, Germany, United Kingdom, Peru, Venezuela, Dominican Republic
estimates.date: Search performed 9 February 2021; videos uploaded 18 March 2020 to 5 February 2021
estimates.measure_type: % of all views of the corpus that went to videos containing hoaxes or conspiracy theories
estimates.value_raw: 616,191 views of the 2 hoax/conspiracy videos out of 57,390,500 total views for all 118 videos = 1.07% (share DERIVED from two verbatim counts; the paper does not state it)
estimates.denominator: 57,390,500 views accumulated by the 118 most-viewed Spanish-language YouTube videos on COVID-19 vaccines (as counted on 9 February 2021)
estimates.definition: Numerator = the view count of the two videos coded as containing hoaxes/conspiracy theories.
estimates.misinfo_def: Video-content category of 'myths and conspiracy theories' / 'hoaxes', coded by two physician raters.
estimates.source_quote: The total amount of views for all videos summed up to 57,390,500 (median [range]: 318,311.5 [150,015–3,975,728]).
estimates.page_loc: Results, p. 3917 (total views) and p. 3918 (hoax video views)
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Same two-physician independent coding as the video-level row; kappa 0.971 reported for message tone only.
estimates.moderator_quote: According to the tone of the message, positive videos accounted for 53.1% of the views, which is proportional to the number of positive videos (53.4%).
estimates.notes: DERIVED value, flagged for the adjudicator: the paper reports the two counts (616,191 hoax-video views; 57,390,500 total views) but never the ratio. It is an exact part/whole share of verbatim counts on the same denominator, which R8 permits, and it is analytically useful because it gives the view-weighted counterpart of the 1.7% item-weighted share - the paper itself makes exactly this item-vs-view comparison for message tone. The 'views' here are cumulative YouTube view counts within a top-N-by-views corpus, so this is a within-corpus exposure share, not the share of Spanish-language COVID-vaccine viewing on YouTube overall. Drop this row if the adjudication rule is that only stated percentages count. Confidence medium. QUOTE NOTE: source_quote gives the denominator sentence, the only contiguous span available; the numerator sentence is quoted in full in the CONTENT row above and in rob.item10_quote ('... garnered 616,191 views, 23,477 likes, 2,458 dislikes and 7,790 comments.').

missed_or_uncertain: 1) NOT extracted (tone, not veracity): message tone was positive in 53.4% of videos, neutral in 32.2%, ambiguous in 13.6% and negative in 1 video (0.8%); positive videos accounted for 53.1% of views. A negative tone means 'arguments were put forward against vaccination', which is a stance and not a falsity judgement, so I did not treat 0.8% (or 0.8% + 13.6%) as a misinformation share. An adjudicator taking a broader 'anti-vaccine content' construct might want the 0.8% row; I judged it out of scope. 2) NOT extracted (corrective content): 15 videos (12.7%) DEBUNKED COVID-19 vaccine hoaxes and conspiracy theories, accumulating 5,172,057 views (9.0% of all views), 267,260 likes (16.4%) and 13,739 dislikes (16.6%). This is counter-misinformation content; the debunked claims are listed (chips, sterility, genetic changes, vaccines cause the disease, pandemic does not exist, needle left in the body, mental deficiency, pharma conspiracy, 5G masks) but they were debunked in these videos, not asserted. 3) NOT extracted (topic composition, Table 4): e.g. safety discussed in 43.2%, target groups 38.9%, adverse effects 38.1%, efficacy 31.4% - topics discussed, not veracity. Note Table 4 does not include a row for myths/conspiracy theories even though the Methods say it was recorded; the 2-video figure appears only in the running text and the abstract. 4) NOT extracted (source composition and engagement): media 57.6% of videos and 55.0% of views; health professionals 16.1% of videos and 18.7% of views; user-generated 23.7%; ORs for positive tone (health professionals vs media OR = 3.09; user-generated vs media OR = 3.02); all view/like/dislike/comment medians and totals in Tables 2 and 3. 5) NO CONCENTRATION row: the paper gives shares of views by source type and by tone, but never a top-X%-of-sources-accounts-for-Y%-of-views statement, and the source categories are content types rather than a ranked top group, so R1 is not met. 6) Sample-size note: the 118 was fixed a priori (6% precision, alpha 5%, expected 88% pro-vaccination videos), i.e. powered for the tone variable, not for a rare hoax outcome.

rob.design: Cross-sectional content analysis of a rank-truncated YouTube corpus. Frame: three Spanish keyword searches ('Vacuna Covid', 'Vacuna coronavirus', 'Vacuna Covid19') run on 9 February 2021 from a cleared browser, results sorted by view count, exclusions applied (unavailable, non-Spanish, duplicate, not about COVID-19 vaccines), and the 118 most-viewed retained; sample size pre-specified for 6% precision, alpha 5%, and an expected 88% proportion of pro-vaccination videos. Videos spanned uploads from 18 March 2020 to 5 February 2021 and 11 countries, dominated by Mexico (35.6%), the USA (15.3%) and Colombia (12.7%). Coding: two authors (physicians) independently viewed every video and recorded upload date, country, source type, publication type, duration, message tone, engagement metrics, and topic presence (benefits, efficacy, costs, safety, adverse effects, contraindications, dosage, target groups, and myths/conspiracy theories). Inter-rater agreement reported for message tone only: complete except for 2 videos, kappa = 0.971, resolved by consensus; no reliability figure for the myths/conspiracy variable. Analysis: descriptive statistics with medians and ranges (normality rejected by Kolmogorov-Smirnov), Mann-Whitney U, Kruskal-Wallis, chi-square/Fisher, univariate logistic regression, SPSS v25, alpha 0.05. No IRB approval required (public videos, no human participants). Key weaknesses for prevalence use: a single day's search on a personalisation-cleared but still algorithmically ordered result list, a top-N-by-views denominator, no fact-checker or source-list ground truth, and only 2 events in the numerator.
